paras: The lynching of John Lynn was the killing of a Black man by a mob of thirty-five armed white men at his home in Assumption Parish, Louisiana, in late July 1888. Lynn shot dead one of the attackers before he was captured, and the mob later shot him in twelve places. A New Orleans telegram presented it as one of a series of 'outrages against the blacks' that had prompted talk of an exodus.

The telegram, dated July 30, placed the parish among areas where repeated outrages against Black residents had become serious enough 'to cause thoughts of an exodus.' It described Lynn as 'a law-abiding colored man' and reported no charge against him.

The mob broke into Lynn's house in the dark, and one of the men was ordered to strike a light. As soon as the light was made, Lynn shot and killed that man from a hiding place in the house. The attackers captured Lynn and left a guard over him while the rest carried away and buried their dead companion. On their return they took Lynn outside and shot him, his body 'perforated in no less than twelve places.'

The telegram stated that the killing became known throughout the parish but that 'the officers of the law have made no effort to capture the midnight marauders.' Neither the attackers nor the dead man were named, and no report of an inquest, arrest or trial was found. Black residents were said to be considering 'a wholesale exodus from the parish' because of 'the entire withdrawal of the protection of the law from them.'

The Omaha Daily Bee printed the account on its front page on July 31 as a special telegram under the headlines 'Another Negro Outrage' and 'Louisiana Whites Murder a Law-Abiding Colored Citizen.' Its correspondent called the killing 'a peculiarly brutal piece of lawlessness.' About ten days later two Dakota weeklies, the Turner County Herald and the Wessington Springs Herald, ran nearly the same text as a brief in an 'At the South' column. No Louisiana paper's report, and no Black-press coverage, was found.

reader.title: Lynching of John Lynn
bases: A mob of thirty-five armed white men broke into a Black man's house, captured him and later shot him to death (A1).

A1 reports that a mob of thirty-five armed white men with no lawful authority captured Lynn and shot him in twelve places, and that officers made no effort to arrest them; the report gives no stated reason for the raid, framing it only among 'outrages against the blacks', and rests on a single telegram (A1).
Every report found is the same New Orleans telegram (A1), reprinted nearly word for word in two Dakota weeklies (A3, A4); no local, independent or follow-up account was found.

accounts.label: New Orleans special telegram
accounts.gist: A mob of thirty-five armed white men broke into Lynn's house; he killed the man who struck a light, was captured, and after the mob buried its dead was taken out and shot in twelve places, with no effort by officers to arrest anyone.

framing.detail: The Omaha Bee headlined the telegram 'Another Negro Outrage' and 'Louisiana Whites Murder a Law-Abiding Colored Citizen', calling it 'a peculiarly brutal piece of lawlessness' and the mob 'midnight marauders'.
Two Dakota weeklies ran the same text without headline or dateline as one brief in an 'At the South' column.

sources.note: New Orleans special telegram dated July 30 (printed 'July 80'), headed 'Another Negro Outrage'; the only original account: 35-man white mob, Lynn kills the man who struck a light, is captured and shot in twelve places; no arrests; exodus talk.
quotes: The house of a law-abiding colored man named John Lynn was broken open and entered by a mob of thirty-five armed white men.
As soon as the light was made, Lynn, from his hiding place in the house, shot and killed the man who made it.
Returning to Lynn they took him out and shot him to pieces, his body being perforated in no less than twelve places.
This act became known all over the parish, but the officers of the law have made no effort to capture the midnight marauders.
The colored people are considering a wholesale exodus from the parish on account of the entire withdrawal of the protection of the law from them.
